publication_scope.blurb: Ludwig Crocius — Book I Chapter 11 On the distribution of sacred theology, from the 1636 Bremen Latin. Densify COMPLETE (PHYS 323–330): parts common and proper; Conrad Bergius's five tractation modes (history, prophecy, invocation, exhortation, didascalia); historical and logical methods; ten divisions of theology including Polanus; analytic distribution into common and proper parts; Liber I corona of six requirements for the theology student as theodidaktos. Liber I ENDED PHYS 330. Liber II starts PHYS 331 (De fine hominis / summum bonum). Cap. 2–10 complete; Cap. 1 tip gap still open.

source_text: CAPUT UNDECIMUM. De S. Theologiae distributione. Hactenus vidimus S. Theologiae definitionem, naturam & principia: sequuntur partes, quarum duae sunt, communis & propria. Cum sacra Theologia sit disciplina practica sui generis, ut supra demonstratum est cap. 1. §. 3. de communi sententia etiam philosophorum, qui optimi ordinis magistri sunt, ordine analytico tractanda est: secundum quem ordinem tum ipsa doctrina tota, tum omnes ejus partes ex fine suo praecipuo tractabuntur, singulaque capita eum locum occupabunt, qui ipsis secundum principalem respectum tum ad totum suum, tum ad finem totius conveniet.
english:
CHAPTER ELEVEN
On the distribution of sacred theology
So far we have seen the definition, nature, and principles of sacred theology.
The parts follow, of which there are two: the common and the proper.

Since sacred theology is a practical discipline of its own kind, as was shown above in chapter 1, section 3, it is to be treated, by the common judgment even of the philosophers who are masters of the best order, in the analytic order.

According to that order both the whole doctrine itself and all its parts will be treated from its chief end, and each head will occupy the place that suits it by principal respect both to its own whole and to the end of the whole.

source_text: Atque, ut hunc primum librum Theologiae nostrae coronide aliqua obsignem, divinum artificium, viamque compendiariam, qua SACRAE LITERAE, tanquam regni Christiani tabulae, veraeque theologiae radices, cum fructu legantur, sub imagine discipuli ingenui hic ostendam. Sex potissimum sunt, quae in discipulo magnis quotidie itineribus, feliciterque profecturo, requiruntur. 1. Aetas, 2. Ingenium, 3. fidus magister, 4. studium & opera fideliter navanda praeceptori, 5. perpetuum exercitium, quo magistro exigenti lectionem exacte recitare possit, 6. reverentia erga praeceptorem. Eadem postulantur a sacrae Theologiae studioso, qui sacras literas, Deique verbum in rem animae suae vertere cupit. Nam is 1. firmum propositum habeat veterem hominem exuendi, ut in Christo fiat homo novus, imo homo Dei, cui sacra scriptura unice destinata est, 2. Tim. 3.16.17. 2. A Deo, DOMINO nostro, intellectum spiritualem, spiritualeque judicium seriis crebrisque gemitibus obnoxie petat, Jacob. 1.5. Luc. 11.9.10.11.12.13. 3. Ad JESUM CHRISTUM, Magistrum cujus cathedra in coelis est, irretortis oculis respectet, eumque recte agnoscat. 4. In hujus divino gymnasio sit assiduus, neque legat duntaxat, sed & lecta relegat, levatisque oculis simul & corde in coelum, quae legit, meditetur atque ruminer. 5. Lectionem unam ex alia perpendat, Magistro coelesti reddat, fundamentum veritatis in ipso solo quaerat, doctrinam ab ipso perceptam interdiu atque inter noctu exerceat, saepe recordetur, & anxie quaerat, ut ipse a seipso indies melior evadat. 6. Sub disciplina & coercitione Christi, spiritusque ejus, coelestis doctoris, perduret; ipsum revereatur, diligat, studiisque suis extra Dei gloriam, animaeque suae salutem nihil quaerat. Hic talis in sacra scriptura & Theologia, sive mysteriis regni Dei, tanquam θεοδίδακτος a Deo doctus, egregiissime proficiet, aeternumque coelo beabitur. Hoc enim proprie necessarium est, ut, qui sacras literas interius & salutariter intelligere, nedum aliis interpretari & cum fructu accommodare cupit, prius resipiscat, Deum revereatur, Christum in regno suo secundum spiritum agnoscere, ejusque vestigia in turba hujus mundi premere velit, spiritumque fidei & sapientiae divinae ardenter petat ab eo, qui discipulorum suorum mentem aperuit, ut intelligerent scripturas, Luc. 24.46.
english: And so that I may seal this first book of our theology with some closing mark, I will here show under the image of a well-born disciple the divine craft and the short way by which the SACRED LETTERS, as the tables of the Christian kingdom and the roots of true theology, may be read with fruit.

Six things especially are required in a disciple who is to advance far and happily by great daily journeys: (1) age, (2) talent, (3) a faithful teacher, (4) study and labor faithfully to be devoted to the instructor, (5) continual exercise by which he can recite the lesson exactly when the teacher demands it, (6) reverence toward the instructor.
The same things are asked of the student of sacred theology who desires to turn the sacred letters and God's Word to the good of his own soul.
For (1) let him have a firm resolve to put off the old man, that in Christ he may become a new man, indeed a man of God, for whom Sacred Scripture is uniquely destined (Second Timothy 3:16–17).
(2) From God our LORD let him humbly ask with earnest and frequent groans for spiritual understanding and spiritual judgment (James 1:5; Luke 11:9–13).
(3) To JESUS CHRIST, the Master whose chair is in the heavens, let him look with unturned eyes and rightly acknowledge him.
(4) In this divine school let him be assiduous, and not only read but reread what he has read, and with eyes and heart lifted together to heaven meditate and ruminate on what he reads.

(5) Let him weigh one reading against another, render it to the heavenly Master, seek the foundation of truth in him alone, practice by day and by night the doctrine received from him, often remember it, and anxiously ask that he himself may daily become better from himself.

(6) Let him endure under the discipline and correction of Christ and of his Spirit, the heavenly teacher; let him revere and love him, and in his studies seek nothing outside God's glory and his own soul's salvation.
Such a one in Sacred Scripture and theology, or the mysteries of God's kingdom, as θεοδίδακτος — taught by God — will advance most excellently and be blessed forever in heaven.

For this is properly necessary: that whoever desires to understand the sacred letters inwardly and savingly, still more to interpret them for others and apply them with fruit, must first repent, revere God, be willing to acknowledge Christ in his kingdom according to the Spirit and to press his footsteps in the crowd of this world, and ardently ask the spirit of faith and of divine wisdom from him who opened his disciples' mind that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:46).

source_text: 1. HISTORICA est, quae quid a Deo, quid ab hominibus datum, imperatum, factum sit ordine enarrat: vaticinia autem, precationes, exhortationes partim ipsi narrationi, prout patitur rerum gestarum ordo, inserens, partim veluti acta quaedam & documenta regni specialia seorsim collocat. Haec methodus non tantum est popularis, sed & naturae subjecti, quod est regnum & quidem certum & singulare, quo videlicet Deus hunc mundum & Ecclesiam praecipue gubernat, apprime conveniens. Quae propterea in sacris literis usurpata est, doctis atque indoctis utilis & necessaria, quibus nullum potius studium esse debet, quam ut TEXTUM SCRIPTURAE intellectu & memoria, quatenus fieri potest, comprehendant, 2. Tim. 3.15. 1. Tim. 4.10.
english: 1. The HISTORICAL is that which narrates in order what has been given, commanded, and done by God and by human beings.
It inserts prophecies, prayers, and exhortations partly into the narration itself, as the order of events allows, and partly sets them apart like certain special acts and documents of the kingdom.

This method is not only popular but also especially fitting to the nature of the subject, which is the kingdom — and a certain and singular one — by which God chiefly governs this world and the Church.

It has therefore been used in the sacred letters, useful and necessary for the learned and the unlearned, for whom no study ought to be preferred to grasping the TEXT OF SCRIPTURE with understanding and memory as far as can be done (Second Timothy 3:15; First Timothy 4:10).

source_text: II. Sunt autem apud praestantes Theologos variae illius tractationes & divisiones. TRACTATIONES de rebus sacris D. Conr. Bergius in laudatis praecognitis suis ad quinque modos refert. PRIMUS est HISTORIA, quae est sermo de factis singularibus praeteritis: in quo temporis potissimum ordo observandus est. SECUNDUS est PROPHETIA, quae est sermo de factis singularibus futuris: in quo partim temporis ordo observatur, partim prudentiae seu congruentiae ad finem particularem, quem Deus vel propheta intendit.
english: II. Among outstanding theologians there are various treatments and divisions of it.
Doctor Conrad Bergius, in his praised Precognita, refers the tractations of sacred things to five modes.
The first is HISTORY, which is discourse about singular past deeds; in it the order of time is chiefly to be observed.

The second is PROPHECY, which is discourse about singular future deeds; in it partly the order of time is observed, partly the prudence or fitness to the particular end that God or the prophet intends.

source_text: 2. LOGICA est, quae partes regni divini earumque actus ad certa genera revocatos apte discernat, & quae in scripturis parallela sparsim occurrunt, ad unum caput coacta inter se conferat: ut utriusque methodi conjunctio intellectui pariter ac memoriae lucem majorem ac praesidium afferat. Haec dupliciter institui potest. Primo, ut praecognito fine doctrinae, & posito subjecto, enumerentur actus, qui sunt media quaedam ad finem, eo fere ordine, quo se mutuo subsequuntur. Quam methodum in compendiis & summis doctrinae Christianae maxime probamus, inque hoc Theologiae enchiridio & idea nostra sequimur. Secundo, actus regni Dei ita enumerari ac dividi possunt, ut differentiae sumantur potissimum a subjectis sive materia regni. Nam habitus & actus specificantur potissimum a subjectis & finibus, ut cap. 1. §. 7. docuimus. Et primo quidem remotae differentiae sumantur a subjectis agentibus: ut, verbi gratia classes locorum communium fiant de actibus Dei, hominis & in specie de actibus & officiis pastorum, parentum, liberorum, magistratuum, subditorum &c. Secundo, propiores differentiae in subjectorum singulorum actibus sumantur ab objectis, in quae tendit actio: v.g. de actibus & officiis hominis erga Deum, erga seipsum, erga proximum, erga amicos, inimicos, pauperes, divites, &c. Tertio, proximae differentiae sumantur a fine sive bono quod intendit actio, & quod a subjecto in subjectum introducitur, v.g. de actibus & officiis hominis erga proximum quod ad bonum intellectus, voluntatis, corporis, cultus externi, &c.
english: 2. The LOGICAL is that which aptly distinguishes the parts of the divine kingdom and their acts recalled to certain genera, and brings together under one head the parallels that occur scattered in the Scriptures, so that the joining of both methods may give greater light and help to understanding and memory alike.
It can be instituted in two ways.

First, when the end of the doctrine is known beforehand and the subject is set, the acts that are certain means to the end are enumerated nearly in the order in which they follow one another — the method we most approve in compendia and summaries of Christian doctrine, and which we follow in this handbook and idea of theology.

Second, the acts of God's kingdom can be so enumerated and divided that differences are taken chiefly from the subjects or matter of the kingdom; for habits and acts are specified chiefly by subjects and ends, as we taught in chapter 1, section 7.

Remote differences are taken from acting subjects (for example common-place classes about the acts of God and of man, and specifically about the acts and offices of pastors, parents, children, magistrates, subjects, and so on); nearer differences in the acts of each subject are taken from the objects toward which the action tends (for example man's acts and offices toward God, himself, neighbor, friends, enemies, the poor, the rich, and so on); nearest differences are taken from the end or good the action intends and introduces from subject into subject (for example man's acts and offices toward the neighbor as to the good of intellect, will, body, outward worship, and so on).
